lab_title: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry in 3D
top_level_objectives: Explain the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron domains around a central atom arrange to minimize mutual repulsion
Identify and distinguish the five fundamental electron-domain geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral)
Predict how lone pairs modify electron-domain geometry to produce molecular geometry (bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal)
Rationalize why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, accounting for bond-angle deviations such as 104.5° in water versus 109.5° in methane
Match VSEPR predictions to the experimentally observed 3D structures of real molecules including H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1 – From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the connection between a 2D Lewis structure and the concept of electron domains, giving students the foundational vocabulary they need before any 3D geometry is introduced.
key_visuals: A flat, glowing 2D Lewis structure of methane (CH4) floating at desk level in AR space
Color-coded highlights that distinguish bonding pairs from lone pairs as the student taps each one
An animated counter in the corner tallying the total number of electron domains around the central carbon
student_actions: Tap each bond and lone pair on the Lewis structure to identify and label it as a bonding domain or lone-pair domain
Confirm the total electron-domain count for carbon in CH4 before advancing
Repeat the domain-counting exercise on a second molecule (water, H2O) that includes lone pairs, reinforcing the distinction

scenes.scene_name: Scene 2 – The Repulsion Principle: Building Intuition
scenes.brief_purpose: Give students a tactile, intuitive feel for why electron domains spread apart, grounding the abstract repulsion principle in a concrete interactive experience before formal geometry names are introduced.
key_visuals: A central atom represented as a glowing sphere floating at chest height in AR
Draggable electron-domain 'lobes' (soft, balloon-like objects) attached to the central atom that visibly compress and glow red when pushed close together
Dynamic arc indicators showing the angles between domains, updating in real time as domains are moved
student_actions: Drag two electron-domain lobes toward each other and observe the red 'repulsion glow' intensify as angles decrease
Release the lobes and watch them automatically settle into the maximum-separation (180°) arrangement
Experiment with adding a third, then a fourth domain and observe the system re-equilibrate each time, building an intuition for angle reduction as domains are added

scenes.brief_purpose: Systematically introduce all five fundamental electron-domain geometries so students can recognize and name them before lone pairs are layered in.
key_visuals: A carousel-style display of five 3D molecular skeletons (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) arranged in an arc the student can walk along in AR space
Each geometry labeled with its name, domain count, and idealized bond angles rendered as floating text
Animated rotation of each model with color-coded bond axes to highlight the symmetry of each arrangement
student_actions: Walk up to or tap each geometry model to trigger a 360° rotation and an audio explanation of why that arrangement minimizes repulsion
Match a set of central-atom domain counts (2 through 6) to the correct geometry shape by dragging cards to the corresponding model
Sketch or mentally note the idealized bond angles before moving on, as these will serve as a reference baseline in later scenes

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4 – Lone Pairs Change the Shape: Building Molecular Geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the critical distinction between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry by systematically replacing bonding domains with lone pairs and observing the resulting shape change.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral electron-domain framework (4 domains) as the starting point, with all four positions initially occupied by identical bonding-pair lobes
A swap interface allowing the student to convert any bonding-pair lobe into a lone-pair lobe (visually larger and more diffuse) one at a time
Side-by-side ghost outlines of the electron-domain geometry versus the molecular geometry (atoms only) updating dynamically as swaps are made, with bond angles displayed
student_actions: Convert one bonding domain to a lone pair, observe the geometry label change from 'tetrahedral' to 'trigonal pyramidal,' and note the bond angle compress slightly
Convert a second bonding domain and observe the further change to 'bent' and additional angle compression toward 104.5°

Repeat the exploration starting from a trigonal bipyramidal framework to discover seesaw, T-shaped, and linear molecular geometries, and from an octahedral framework to find square pyramidal and square planar

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5 – Why Lone Pairs Take Up More Space: The Angle Deviation Deep Dive
scenes.brief_purpose: Provide a mechanistic explanation for why lone pairs exert greater repulsion than bonding pairs, accounting for real-world bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
key_visuals: A side-by-side AR comparison of the NH3 (trigonal pyramidal, 107°) and CH4 (tetrahedral, 109.5°) models at the same scale
Electron-density cloud visualizations showing the lone pair on nitrogen as a broader, more diffuse lobe compared to the narrower N–H bonding lobes
Animated 'pressure arrows' of different sizes emanating from lone-pair versus bonding-pair domains to represent their relative repulsive force
student_actions: Tap the lone-pair lobe on NH3 to read a tooltip explaining that lone pairs are held only by one nucleus and therefore spread out more, increasing repulsion on neighboring bonds
Drag a slider that gradually increases lone-pair 'size' on a generic AX3E model and watch the H–A–H angle decrease in real time, connecting the visual to the numerical angle value
Answer a checkpoint question predicting whether the H–O–H angle in water should be larger or smaller than the H–N–H angle in ammonia, and receive immediate AR feedback

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6 – Real Molecule Gallery: VSEPR Predictions vs. Observation
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding by asking students to predict the geometry of a set of real molecules and then compare their predictions with experimentally determined 3D structures.
key_visuals: A gallery wall of six molecule 'cards' (H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4) displayed as AR holograms the student can pick up and examine from any angle
Each molecule card initially showing only the Lewis structure; the 3D structure is revealed only after the student makes a prediction
Experimental bond-angle data and a brief 'real-world relevance' note (e.g., the bent shape of water and its consequences for polarity) appearing alongside the confirmed 3D structure
student_actions: For each molecule card, count the electron domains, select the electron-domain geometry, then select the molecular geometry from a multiple-choice overlay before flipping the card
Rotate and inspect the revealed 3D model, comparing it to their prediction and reading the experimental bond angles
Flag any molecule whose geometry surprised them; these flags feed into the reflection scene that follows

scenes.brief_purpose: Provide an open-ended, hands-on synthesis task where students construct a target molecule geometry from scratch, integrating every skill developed in earlier scenes.
key_visuals: An empty AR workspace with a central atom and a toolkit of draggable bonding-pair lobes and lone-pair lobes
A target molecule name and Lewis structure shown in a small AR panel to the side (e.g., XeF4 or BrF5)
A real-time geometry validator that highlights the model green when the correct arrangement is achieved and red when it is not, with an angle readout
student_actions: Drag the correct number and type of electron domains onto the central atom for the assigned target molecule

Arrange the domains to minimize repulsion, paying special attention to where lone pairs should be placed to achieve the lowest-energy configuration (e.g., equatorial vs. axial positions in the bipyramidal family)
Submit the completed model for scoring, then compare it to the reference structure and read targeted feedback explaining any placement errors

scenes.scene_name: Scene 8 – Summary and Concept Map Wrap-Up
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the full arc of the lab by having students reconstruct the logical chain from Lewis structure → electron domains → electron-domain geometry → molecular geometry, reinforcing retention and transfer.
key_visuals: An interactive AR concept map with floating nodes for each major term (Lewis structure, electron domain, bonding pair, lone pair, electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, bond angle) connected by labeled arrows
Thumbnail 3D models of all major shapes orbiting the map as visual anchors
A personal 'lab record' panel summarizing the molecules the student successfully predicted during the session
student_actions: Drag and connect missing arrows on the concept map to complete the logical relationships between terms, receiving confirmation chimes for correct connections
Review their flagged 'surprise' molecules from the gallery scene and read short explanations resolving each one

Complete a three-question exit quiz embedded in the AR environment — predicting the geometry and approximate bond angle of one novel molecule not seen earlier in the lab — to assess independent transfer of learning
